cards.scenario: Many accounts; centralize identities and permissions, synced with on-prem IdP.
cards.ok: Central-account SAML IdP mapped to IAM roles; cross-account role access.
cards.bad: Separate SAML provider and IAM roles configured in every account.
cards.why: One central federation point centralizes identity and permissions; per-account setups or Lambda replication do not.

cards.scenario: Dev accounts need fixed budgets and no expensive services.
cards.ok: Budget + SCP denying costly services + SNS-triggered Lambda to terminate resources.
cards.bad: SCP that defines a fixed monthly resource usage limit.
cards.why: SCPs only allow or deny actions, never cap spend; built-in Budgets actions only stop EC2/RDS or attach policies.

cards.scenario: IAM user with S3 read-only policy gets access denied in a member account.
cards.ok: Check OU service control policies + the user's permissions boundary.
cards.bad: Check bucket policies and bucket ACLs.
cards.why: ListAllMyBuckets is account-level; bucket policies/ACLs never control it. SCPs and permissions boundaries cap IAM permissions.

cards.scenario: Block many services org-wide, yet allow per-business-unit exceptions with minimal overhead.
cards.ok: Deny-list SCP at OU level, keep default allow; exception OU gets an SCP denying fewer services.
cards.bad: Allow-list SCP at root; remove default allow; add allowed services per OU.
cards.why: Allow lists need explicit allows at every level (high overhead); deny lists keep the default allow.

cards.scenario: Organizations with management, production, development accounts; audit all API actions.
cards.ok: Centralized CloudTrail logging (org trail) + users in member accounts, not management.
cards.bad: Create all resources in the management account, granting members access.
cards.why: Management account only for org-level tasks; workloads and users live in member accounts (modern: Log Archive account, Identity Center).

cards.scenario: Single bill per business unit plus central limits on allowed services.
cards.ok: One organization in parent account (all features) + SCP allowing approved services.
cards.bad: Permissions boundaries applied to each business-unit account.
cards.why: Boundaries attach to IAM identities, not accounts; SCPs centrally cap member accounts.

cards.scenario: Mobile app uses custom-built authentication and IAM roles for authorization.
cards.ok: Custom SAML IdP with LDAP via IAM provider + custom OIDC with Cognito.
cards.bad: Custom LDAP connector with API Gateway and a Lambda JWT authorizer.
cards.why: Roles need IAM SAML/OIDC federation or Cognito identity pools; a Lambda authorizer issues no IAM credentials.

cards.scenario: Prod and test accounts need centrally controlled identities and permissions.
cards.ok: Separate identity account; roles in prod/test trust it.
cards.bad: IAM users in prod and test accounts, controlled by SCPs.
cards.why: Best practice: users in one identity account assume cross-account roles. SCPs do not grant permissions.

cards.scenario: Only the management account may buy Reserved Instances, including future accounts.
cards.ok: Deny ec2:PurchaseReservedInstancesOffering SCP attached to the organization root.
cards.bad: Deny SCP attached to a new OU of current members.
cards.why: Root attachment is inherited by all current and future accounts; SCPs skip the management account.

cards.scenario: Multi-account landing zone with guardrails, AD login and minimal custom work.
cards.ok: Control Tower landing zone + Account Factory + IAM Identity Center with AD.
cards.bad: Manual Organizations accounts with SAML federation per account.
cards.why: Control Tower automates governance and guardrails; manual accounts add per-account setup overhead.

cards.scenario: Large daily S3 image volume flows through NAT gateways; cut cost, stay secure.
cards.ok: S3 gateway endpoint with endpoint policy scoped to the bucket.
cards.bad: Move EC2 to public subnets and remove NAT gateways.
cards.why: Gateway endpoint is free and keeps S3 traffic off NAT; NAT still serves other internet access.

cards.scenario: 15 VPCs plus Direct Connect need transitive connectivity, least complexity.
cards.ok: Transit gateway with VPC attachments + DX gateway attached to the transit gateway.
cards.bad: Full-mesh VPC peering + DX gateway associated with a VGW per VPC.
cards.why: Transit gateway gives transitive hub routing; peering is not transitive and meshes get complex.

cards.scenario: Enable IPv6; public subnets stay reachable, private instances stay unreachable from the internet.
cards.ok: IPv6 CIDRs; public routes ::/0 to internet gateway, private routes ::/0 to egress-only gateway.
cards.bad: Route ::/0 for public and private subnets through the existing NAT gateway.
cards.why: IPv4 NAT gateways do not handle IPv6; egress-only gateway allows outbound IPv6 but blocks inbound.

cards.scenario: Private hosted zone in management account must resolve from new production VPC.
cards.ok: Create association authorization in owner account, then associate the production VPC.
cards.bad: Create a second private hosted zone and configure Route 53 cross-account replication.
cards.why: Cross-account association needs owner authorization, then association from the VPC account; Route 53 has no replication.

cards.scenario: Custom TCP port app needs fixed whitelisted IPs, multi-AZ, behind a DNS name.
cards.ok: One Elastic IP per AZ on an NLB, plus alias A record.
cards.bad: ECS public IPs behind an Application Load Balancer.
cards.why: NLB handles TCP with static EIPs per AZ; ALB is HTTP/S with no static IPs.

cards.scenario: Offer on-premises IT services to other AWS customers over Direct Connect, no internet.
cards.ok: VPC endpoint service behind an NLB (TCP), reached over DX.
cards.bad: VPC endpoint service fronted by an Application Load Balancer.
cards.why: PrivateLink endpoint services require an NLB (or GWLB); the NLB can target on-premises IPs.

cards.scenario: On-premises app writes DynamoDB; needs multi-Region and consistent network performance.
cards.ok: Second DX connection + DynamoDB global tables, app fails over.
cards.bad: Managed VPN to second Region with Streams and Lambda copy.
cards.why: VPN rides the internet so performance varies; global tables replicate natively.

cards.scenario: Latency routing sends users to a Region whose RDS is blocked; no failover occurred.
cards.ok: Custom health check on DB endpoints + Evaluate Target Health on latency aliases.
cards.bad: Switch to failover routing active-active with ALB checks.
cards.why: Health checks never tested the database; add DB-level checks and target health to latency records.

cards.scenario: Paris web app with NAS and MySQL moves to AWS: 99.9% SLA, Europe and US latency.
cards.ok: One Region, three AZs: ALB, ASG, ElastiCache, Aurora Multi-AZ, EFS, CloudFront.
cards.bad: Two Regions with three AZs each and global database.
cards.why: Multi-AZ in one Region meets 99.9%; CloudFront serves US users. Extra Region only adds cost.

cards.scenario: Serverless global web app: low latency, baseline DDoS protection, social login.
cards.ok: API Gateway + Lambda, S3 static site behind CloudFront, Cognito for social login.
cards.bad: API Gateway + Lambda with S3 static site, WAF web ACL for DDoS, no CloudFront.
cards.why: Global low latency needs CloudFront edge caching, which includes Shield Standard; WAF adds no edge delivery.

cards.scenario: Members download all files in a CloudFront-fronted private S3 bucket.
cards.ok: CloudFront signed cookies set by the application.
cards.bad: Signed URL generated per file.
cards.why: Signed cookies grant access to many files without changing URLs; signed URLs fit one file each.

cards.scenario: Bursts of identical API requests overload Aurora behind API Gateway and Lambda.
cards.ok: Edge-optimized endpoint plus API Gateway stage caching.
cards.bad: Larger Aurora instance with more memory.
cards.why: Stage caching absorbs repeated queries before Lambda or the database; scaling up only masks it.

cards.scenario: CloudFront cache hit ratio falls: query strings arrive unordered and mixed-case.
cards.ok: Lambda@Edge viewer-request function sorting and lowercasing query strings.
cards.bad: WAF web ACL rewriting URLs to lowercase through Lambda.
cards.why: WAF cannot rewrite requests; normalizing at viewer request makes cache keys consistent. (Today CloudFront Functions is the lighter fit.)

cards.scenario: CloudFront with S3 website endpoint origin returns 403 Access Denied.
cards.ok: Check S3 Block Public Access + check SSE-KMS encryption on objects.
cards.bad: Check object lock, versioning or storage class.
cards.why: Website endpoint needs public objects and no KMS encryption; Block Public Access overrides.

cards.scenario: European users upload images slowly to a bucket in us-west-1.
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration + multipart upload.
cards.bad: CloudFront with S3 origin, or byte-range fetches.
cards.why: Transfer Acceleration uses edge locations; multipart parallelises uploads. CloudFront and ranges are downloads.

cards.scenario: 10-node Linux HPC cluster needs low-latency, high-speed inter-node networking.
cards.ok: Cluster placement group + EFA-capable instance types.
cards.bad: Partition placement group + instances spread across three AZs.
cards.why: Cluster group packs nodes close in one AZ for low latency; EFA accelerates HPC traffic.

cards.scenario: Java app with MySQL and local sessions needs high availability.
cards.ok: ElastiCache sessions behind ALB + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + Auto Scaling group.
cards.bad: Self-managed MySQL on EC2 with a Multi-AZ setting.
cards.why: Externalize sessions, use managed Multi-AZ database, self-healing ASG; Multi-AZ is an RDS feature.

cards.scenario: TypeScript/JavaScript developers want infrastructure as code without learning new languages.
cards.ok: Define resources in TypeScript with AWS CDK; synthesize CloudFormation in a CodeBuild stage.
cards.bad: AWS SAM with the application code embedded as template metadata.
cards.why: CDK synthesizes CloudFormation from real languages; SAM is serverless-only and metadata cannot run code.

cards.scenario: Private GitHub repo, Jenkins builds; alert on failed builds, zero-downtime deploys, easy rollback.
cards.ok: GitHub webhooks trigger CodePipeline; Jenkins CodeBuild plugin tests; SNS alerts; CodeDeploy blue/green.
cards.bad: GitHub websockets trigger the pipeline; X-Ray used for unit testing.
cards.why: CodePipeline is triggered by webhooks, not websockets; X-Ray traces requests and does not run tests.

cards.scenario: ECS cluster: minimize instance cost while limiting interruption risk.
cards.ok: Spot instances with Spot Instance Draining enabled.
cards.bad: Reserved instances with termination protection.
cards.why: Spot is cheapest; draining moves tasks off on the two-minute interruption notice. Reserved costs more.

cards.scenario: Migrate 10-node HPC cluster with high-speed inter-node connectivity.
cards.ok: Placement group (cluster) + EFA-capable instances.
cards.bad: Instances across multiple AZs + burstable performance instances.
cards.why: Tightly coupled HPC needs nodes close together; EFA cuts latency; multi-AZ adds latency.

cards.scenario: CodeDeploy for Lambda: send the update to a subset of users first.
cards.ok: Canary deployment: small traffic percentage first, remainder after an interval.
cards.bad: Linear deployment.
cards.why: Canary shifts in two steps (small share, then the rest); linear shifts in equal increments.

cards.scenario: Lambda updates through CloudFormation caused outages; need gradual traffic shifting.
cards.ok: Alias with weighted routing-config via update-alias for canary traffic.
cards.bad: update-function-configuration with routing-config on new versions.
cards.why: Weighted traffic shifting is an alias feature set with update-alias; function configuration does not route traffic.

cards.scenario: Modernized app needs multiple releases per hour and easy rollback via CI/CD.
cards.ok: Elastic Beanstalk blue/green: deploy to a secondary environment, swap CNAMEs.
cards.bad: Bake AMIs and replace Auto Scaling instances in a staged approach.
cards.why: CNAME swap is instant and reversible; AMI rebake and instance replacement is too slow for hourly releases.

cards.scenario: ECS image needs a manual tool update; automate image rebuild on code change.
cards.ok: ECR repo + CodeBuild rebuilds image + CodePipeline from tool code source triggers CodeBuild.
cards.bad: CodeDeploy application that builds the updated container image.
cards.why: CodeBuild builds images, CodeDeploy only deploys. CodeCommit availability has shifted; pattern holds with any Git source.

cards.scenario: Quickly enable 350 remote staff: existing AD logins, MFA, familiar desktop UI.
cards.ok: WorkSpaces with AD Connector over VPN and a RADIUS server for MFA.
cards.bad: AppStream 2.0 streaming apps, integrated with AD FS and MFA.
cards.why: WorkSpaces gives full desktops matching the office; AppStream streams individual apps. AD Connector + RADIUS gives MFA.

cards.scenario: Template changes via CodePipeline risk downtime in an Auto Scaling group app.
cards.ok: CodeBuild tests + CloudFormation change sets preview + CodeDeploy blue/green.
cards.bad: CodeCommit source with CodeBuild tests and CloudFormation StackSets updates.
cards.why: Change sets preview replacements before deploy; blue/green avoids downtime; StackSets is multi-account deployment, not safety.

cards.scenario: Many CodeBuild projects re-download a large third-party S3 dataset, slowing the pipeline.
cards.ok: S3 cache for CodeBuild with the data directory in the cache definition.
cards.bad: EFS in a new VPC mounted at the data directory.
cards.why: S3 cache persists across builds and hosts; EFS adds VPC, cost and copying of third-party data.

cards.scenario: S3 uploads from ECS tasks suddenly return 403; bucket policy and roles unchanged.
cards.ok: ECS task IAM role was modified.
cards.bad: Tasks have insufficient memory assigned.
cards.why: 403 is authorization; best practice puts S3 permissions in the task role. Memory never causes 403.

cards.scenario: Fargate task in private subnet fails pulling ECR image: CannotPullContainerError.
cards.ok: Auto-assign public IP disabled, NAT gateway in a public subnet.
cards.bad: NAT gateway placed in a private subnet.
cards.why: Task ENI needs an internet route; the NAT must sit in a public subnet.

cards.scenario: Speed up Lambda version rollout and error detection for serverless API.
cards.ok: AWS SAM with CodeDeploy gradual traffic shifting, pre/post-traffic hooks, alarm rollback.
cards.bad: Consolidate the CLI scripts into one deploy-and-revert script.
cards.why: CodeDeploy shifts Lambda aliases gradually and auto-rolls back on CloudWatch alarms.

cards.scenario: Sensor Lambda slows past 2 minutes and throws TooManyRequestsException.
cards.ok: Increase Lambda memory + buffer API data in Kinesis with batch processing.
cards.bad: Increase Lambda CPU units or use an SQS FIFO trigger.
cards.why: Lambda CPU scales with memory; Kinesis buffering tames concurrency throttling.

cards.scenario: Orders processed immediately, in order, always available, variable load.
cards.ok: SQS FIFO queue with Reserved Instances across multiple AZs.
cards.bad: SQS FIFO queue with Spot Instances across multiple AZs.
cards.why: FIFO queue preserves order; Spot can be reclaimed, risking availability; SNS is notification, not queueing.

cards.scenario: Credit-card feed in S3 needs automatic masking and JSON conversion on delivery.
cards.ok: S3 event triggers Lambda that starts a Glue ETL job to mask and output JSON.
cards.bad: Athena query on delivery that starts an EMR ETL job.
cards.why: Glue ETL is serverless and built for batch transforms; Athena queries do not launch EMR jobs.

cards.scenario: Thousands of sensors at 8 KB/s each; near-real-time analytics, durable, warehouse output.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams with Kinesis clients analyzing, results loaded to Redshift.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Firehose with Kinesis clients, results saved to RDS.
cards.why: Streams is durable with custom consumers for real-time analysis; Firehose only delivers to destinations.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB auto scaling at 70% still throttles during short predictable write bursts.
cards.ok: Application Auto Scaling scheduled action to raise write capacity before the peaks.
cards.bad: CloudWatch Events monitors the dead letter queue and Lambda retries failed records.
cards.why: Reactive scaling lags sudden spikes; scheduled scaling pre-provisions for predictable peaks; retries add no capacity.

cards.scenario: Weekday upload surges; scale image processing and notify users when done.
cards.ok: S3 event to SQS + Lambda consumer + SNS push notification.
cards.bad: S3 events to an Amazon MQ queue, S3 Batch Operations for processing.
cards.why: S3 to SQS to Lambda decouples and scales with load; Batch Operations is not event-driven processing.

cards.scenario: IoT JSON data, ODBC analytics tool, compute bottleneck; migrate cost-effectively.
cards.ok: S3 + Glue transform + Glue Data Catalog + Athena for ODBC queries.
cards.bad: S3 + Lambda transform + DynamoDB global table.
cards.why: Serverless S3, Glue and Athena remove compute limits and support ODBC; DynamoDB is not an analytics warehouse.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB slows at peak with no errors; improve with minimal application changes.
cards.ok: DynamoDB auto scaling + DAX cache cluster.
cards.bad: ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of the table.
cards.why: Auto scaling adds capacity and DAX is a drop-in cache; ElastiCache and retry logic need code changes.

cards.scenario: Web fleet fires async metadata jobs; scale to tens of thousands in under a minute, cheaply.
cards.ok: SQS queue as Lambda event source.
cards.bad: Step Functions invoked for every job.
cards.why: SQS plus Lambda is serverless, buffered and cheap; Step Functions adds per-transition cost.

cards.scenario: Scale photo processing and delivery globally, cost-effectively.
cards.ok: Lambda for image processing + CloudFront in front of the S3 images.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling group for EC2 processing or move all to ECS.
cards.why: Lambda is cheap and scales massively; CloudFront caches images at the edge globally.

cards.scenario: Move REST API with session data to AWS; keep API model, scale with variable load.
cards.ok: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB on-demand.
cards.bad: ALB with Lambda and DynamoDB on-demand.
cards.why: API Gateway preserves the REST API model; ALB lacks API management features.

cards.scenario: Log all DynamoDB item changes within 30 minutes to catch fraud.
cards.ok: DynamoDB Streams to Lambda, Kinesis, analytics and SNS.
cards.bad: CloudTrail API events filtered for anomalies.
cards.why: CloudTrail logs control-plane calls, not item-level data changes; Streams capture each modification.

cards.scenario: 150 VMs, 50 TB, saturated internet; critical VMs need minimal downtime.
cards.ok: Direct Connect private VIF plus Application Migration Service (MGN) replication.
cards.bad: Export VMs, ship via Snowball, then VM Import/Export.
cards.why: MGN replicates continuously for minimal cutover downtime; Snowball export leaves VMs offline for days.

cards.scenario: Move 25 TB to S3 urgently; 1 Gbps internet, 500 Mbps Direct Connect.
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration over the faster internet link.
cards.bad: Copy data to an 80 TB Snowball device.
cards.why: Internet link outruns Direct Connect; Snowball shipping both ways takes longer than uploading.

cards.scenario: DR site in a second Region: EC2/ELB web tier, S3 images, DynamoDB data.
cards.ok: Route 53 health-check failover + S3 cross-Region replication + DynamoDB global tables.
cards.bad: DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda copy, or multi-Region ELB targets.
cards.why: ELBs are Regional; global tables and CRR replicate natively, Route 53 fails over.

cards.scenario: Failed S3 multipart backups keep raising storage costs.
cards.ok: Multipart upload + lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads.
cards.bad: Multipart upload + lifecycle archive to Glacier daily.
cards.why: Incomplete parts are invisible, not objects; only AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle removes them.

cards.scenario: RDS MySQL needing multi-Region availability with the highest practical resilience.
cards.ok: Cross-Region read replica, promote on outage.
cards.bad: RDS global tables or multi-master across Regions.
cards.why: Global tables are DynamoDB only; RDS MySQL has no cross-Region multi-master.

cards.scenario: Map on-premises dependencies and right-size VMware plus physical servers for migration.
cards.ok: ADS Connector in vCenter + Discovery Agent on physical servers.
cards.bad: Discovery Agent only on every system, or import a CMDB.
cards.why: Connector covers VMware VMs; agents add dependencies and performance. Connector now succeeded by Agentless Collector.

cards.scenario: Small 100GB gp RDS slows at peak with low CPU, ample memory and free space.
cards.ok: I/O credit balance exhausted on small General Purpose SSD volume.
cards.bad: Network bandwidth of the instance was exhausted.
cards.why: gp2 gives 3 IOPS/GB and bursts on credits; gp3 now has none.

cards.scenario: Move 150 custom VMs and 50TB NAS in 90 days, minimal downtime.
cards.ok: Application Migration Service for VMs + Storage Gateway for NAS data.
cards.bad: Reinstall applications on new EC2 instances.
cards.why: MGN replicates block-level for near-zero downtime; Storage Gateway moves NAS data over the idle link.

cards.scenario: Two-tier app must be highly available across three AZs in one Region.
cards.ok: Aurora writer plus Aurora Replicas in two other AZs.
cards.bad: Aurora Global Database.
cards.why: Aurora storage spans 3 AZs and replicas fail over; Global Database is cross-Region DR.

cards.scenario: 15TB database: RPO under 5 minutes, RTO under 15 minutes, cheap cross-Region failover.
cards.ok: RDS cross-Region read replica, promote on failure.
cards.bad: Aurora with DMS replication between Regional clusters.
cards.why: Async replica gives low RPO and fast promotion; DMS adds a second cluster's cost.

cards.scenario: Fargate and RDS MySQL app needs fast DR recovery in another Region.
cards.ok: Warm standby ECS plus cross-Region read replica; Lambda promotes it, updates Route 53.
cards.bad: Rebuild ECS and restore RDS from copied snapshots after failure.
cards.why: Replica promotion beats snapshot restore for RTO; standby ECS shortens recovery.

cards.scenario: Back up EBS data to company S3 bucket with no SSH access, minimal app impact.
cards.ok: Data Lifecycle Manager snapshot, then EBS direct APIs copy to S3.
cards.bad: Session Manager to the live instance, copy data to S3.
cards.why: Snapshot-based backup avoids touching the critical instance; DLM automates snapshots.

cards.scenario: 403 from S3 through VPC endpoint; bucket uses SSE-KMS; IAM S3 permissions verified.
cards.ok: Verify the role has permission to use the bucket's KMS key.
cards.bad: Verify the role's trust relationship.
cards.why: Role was already assumed, so trust works; KMS-encrypted objects also need kms:Decrypt on the key.

cards.scenario: EC2 in private subnet writes to one S3 bucket; no internet, only app instances.
cards.ok: Gateway endpoint policy limited to the bucket + bucket policy allowing only the instance role.
cards.bad: Endpoint policy to the bucket + bucket policy allowing only the VPC endpoint.
cards.why: Endpoint-only bucket policy admits anything in the VPC via that endpoint; a role principal restricts to app instances.

cards.scenario: Lambda to Aurora MySQL in dev and prod; no hardcoded credentials, automated rotation.
cards.ok: Secrets Manager secret per environment with automatic rotation enabled.
cards.bad: Credentials stored in KMS with automatic key rotation.
cards.why: Secrets Manager rotates database passwords natively; KMS manages keys, and key rotation is not password rotation.

cards.scenario: Confidential S3 bucket: identify requester IPs and auto-remediate policy changes.
cards.ok: S3 server access logs queried in Athena + Config rule with auto-remediation.
cards.bad: Macie to identify request IPs and remediate bucket policy changes.
cards.why: Access logs record requester IPs; Config auto-remediation reverses policy drift. Macie classifies data, not request IPs.

cards.scenario: Lock down security groups for ALB fronting private-subnet EC2 instances.
cards.ok: WebAppSG allows port 80 from ALB-SG + ALB-SG allows 80 from 0.0.0.0/0.
cards.bad: ALB-SG allowing port 80 inbound from WebAppSG.
cards.why: Clients reach the ALB from anywhere; instances admit only the ALB security group.

cards.scenario: Detect and remediate IAM secret keys committed to CodeCommit continuously.
cards.ok: CodeCommit trigger invokes Lambda to scan pushes, disable keys and notify.
cards.bad: Trusted Advisor check then Secrets Manager rotation.
cards.why: Trusted Advisor does not scan repositories; a push trigger inspects commits.

cards.scenario: Biweekly CSV of Lambda memory and cost recommendations, least development.
cards.ok: Compute Optimizer ExportLambdaFunctionRecommendations to S3, scheduled via EventBridge.
cards.bad: Custom Lambda collating CloudWatch Logs metrics into a CSV report.
cards.why: Compute Optimizer already computes memory/cost recommendations and exports CSV; no analysis code needed.

cards.scenario: Add cost-center and project tags on all new EC2/RDS across Organizations efficiently.
cards.ok: Tag Editor + cost allocation tags + SCP denying creation without required tags.
cards.bad: Permissions boundaries restricting untagged resource creation.
cards.why: SCPs enforce tags org-wide on new resources; boundaries attach per identity.

cards.scenario: Right-sized EC2 ASG and RDS on On-Demand; cut cost without hurting reliability.
cards.ok: Reserve RDS and the always-running baseline EC2 instances.
cards.bad: Spot Instances for RDS and the EC2 fleet.
cards.why: RDS can't use Spot; reservations fit steady baseline, On-Demand covers spikes.

cards.scenario: Alert at 80% quota use, checked every 15 minutes, across Regions.
cards.ok: Trusted Advisor via scheduled EventBridge + Lambda + SNS.
cards.bad: Same flow alerting through AWS Budgets.
cards.why: Budgets track cost, not quotas; periodic Config can't run every 15 min. Modern: Service Quotas AWS/Usage alarm.
